Artificial turf terms explained: face weight, infill, thatch, stimp

This glossary defines the terms that show up on a Florida turf quote or spec sheet as of September 2026, from face weight and denier to drip line and PFAS, grouped by product, base, installation, putting greens, pets and law, with each term linked to the page that covers it in full.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Artificial turf terms explained

This glossary defines the terms that show up on a Florida turf quote or spec sheet, grouped by product, base, installation, putting greens, pets and law, from face weight and denier to drip line and PFAS. A putting green quote and a sports-turf bid tend to use the widest mix of these terms in one document, which is where a glossary like this earns its keep.

Test standards behind common spec numbers
SpecWhat it measuresTest standard
Face weightWeight of yarn fiber per square yard, not the backingASTM D5848
Pile heightBlade length from the backing to the tipASTM D5793
DenierThickness of an individual yarn fiberASTM D1907
Tuft bindPull force before a tufted blade releases from the backingASTM D1335

Synthetic Turf Council performance guidelines lists the full set of test methods manufacturers use.

Product terms

  • Face weight. How much yarn sits on a square yard of backing, in ounces; heavier generally means denser and longer-wearing turf.
  • Pile height. How tall the blades stand, from about 0.4 in on a putting surface to 2 in on a full, plush lawn. The full by-use table breaks this down by application.
  • Gauge. The spacing between tufted rows, commonly 3/8 to 5/8 in; a tighter gauge packs more yarn into the same area.
  • Denier. The thickness of a single yarn fiber; a higher denier resists matting and holds its shape longer under sun and traffic.
  • Tuft bind. The force needed to pull one tufted blade out of the backing; low tuft bind shows up years later as bald, thinning patches.
  • Thatch. Curled fiber tufted in at the base of the blades to add body and a more natural look, similar to dead grass mixed into a real lawn.
  • Backing. The material the yarn is tufted into; a primary backing holds the tufts, and a secondary coating locks them in place.
  • UV stabilization. Additives built into the yarn that slow color loss and brittleness from sun exposure, the difference between a lawn that fades in years and one that fades in a decade or more.

Base and drainage terms

  • Subgrade. The native soil beneath the base rock; Florida's 2026 rule requires it not be compacted so hard that it hurts percolation.
  • Base rock. Washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete laid under the turf; "washed" means fines have been rinsed out so the material doesn't bind into a crust.
  • Compaction, in lifts. Compacting base material in more than one thin layer rather than one thick pass, which produces a firmer, more even base.
  • Percolation. How well water moves down through soil; a subgrade compacted too hard percolates poorly and can pool water under the base.
  • Permeable backing. A backing perforated to let water pass through rather than pool on top; required under the state's 2026 material standard.
  • Positive grade. A slope, typically 1-2%, that carries water away from the house instead of toward it.
  • Weed barrier. A fabric layer sometimes placed under the base to slow weed growth; usually skipped under pet turf because it can trap urine against the base.

Installation terms

  • Seam. The joint between two turf panels, joined with tape and adhesive and matched for grain direction so the join disappears into the pile.
  • Grain direction. Which way the blades lean on a roll of turf; mismatched grain across a seam shows up as a visible line or color shift.
  • Perimeter anchor. Nails, staples or a bender-board edge securing the turf's outer edge; Florida's rule requires anchoring at all edges and seams to withstand wind or flooding.
  • Infill. Granular material brushed between the blades to hold the backing down and keep fibers standing; limited to natural or coated sand on a Florida lawn.
  • Silica sand. The standard, natural infill material for a lawn; rounded silica grains help fibers stand without excess heat retention.
  • Zeolite. A natural mineral infill that helps neutralize pet-urine odor between rinses, common in pet-turf builds.
  • Coated sand. Silica sand with a functional coating, such as an antimicrobial or cooling treatment; the coating has to be non-toxic to comply with the state rule.

Putting green terms

  • Stimp speed. A measurement of how far a ball rolls on a green; most home greens land in the 8-10 range, slower than a tournament green. The putting green cost guide has more on what shapes a home build.
  • Cup and flag. The actual hole and marker set into a green, priced separately from the turf and base beneath it.
  • Fringe / collar. The longer-pile turf bordering a putting surface, transitioning it visually into the surrounding lawn.
  • Contouring. A shaped subbase built to add slope and break to a green's roll, priced separately from a flat installation.
  • Chipping pad. A separate turf zone with a taller pile than the putting surface, built for a wedge to interact with the way it would on real fairway grass.

Pet terms

  • Odor-control infill. Zeolite or an antimicrobial coated sand chosen specifically to manage ammonia buildup between rinses. The pet turf page covers the full build.
  • Flush-and-drain. Rinsing a pet area thoroughly enough that liquid moves through the backing and base rather than sitting on the surface.
  • No weed barrier. A deliberate choice on pet-turf builds, since a fabric layer under the base can trap urine against it instead of letting it drain through.

Law and paperwork terms

  • Drip line. The ring on the ground beneath a tree's outermost branches, used to estimate its protected root zone. This page covers how it applies to turf.
  • Setback. A required distance from a feature, such as the 10-foot setback Florida's rule sets from a lake, pond or canal.
  • PFAS. A class of manufactured chemicals; Florida's 2026 rule bars any intentionally added PFAS in turf, backing or infill.
  • Certified arborist. A tree-care professional credentialed to certify that a specific project, such as turf near a drip line, won't harm a protected tree.
  • ARC. An architectural review committee, the HOA body that approves visible exterior changes; the HOA rules page covers what it can and can't require.
  • Rule 62-308.100. Florida's DEP synthetic turf standard, effective May 19, 2026, setting minimum material and installation requirements for single-family lots of one acre or less.
  • Local business tax receipt. A county or city tax registration for operating a business locally; not a skills license, but worth checking before hiring.

A worked example

Say you have a quote that lists "80 oz, 1.75 in, C-shape blade, coated silica infill" for a 900 sq ft backyard. That's a face weight of 80 ounces per square yard, a 1.75-inch pile height, a curved blade profile sold for a fuller look, and infill that's silica sand carrying a functional coating, most likely for odor control or a mild cooling effect. Reading a spec sheet this way turns four glossary terms into an actual picture of what's going down in the yard, rather than four numbers to take on faith.

Questions people ask

What's the difference between face weight and total weight on a spec sheet?

Face weight counts only the yarn fiber per square yard; total weight adds the backing material back in. A spec sheet that lists only one of the two isn't necessarily hiding anything, but ask which figure you're looking at before comparing two products.

Why do two turf products with the same pile height feel different underfoot?

Face weight, denier and blade shape all affect how dense and springy a lawn feels, so two products can share a pile height while differing noticeably in hand feel and how quickly the blades spring back after foot traffic.

Is stimp speed the same measurement pro golfers use?

Yes, the same stimpmeter method, though a home green's turf and infill are tuned more for durability outdoors than for matching a tournament green's faster, more delicate surface.

Does a manufacturer ever list denier without listing face weight?

Some do, since the two measure different things: denier is about individual fiber thickness, and face weight is about total yarn density. A complete spec sheet lists both, along with pile height and backing type.
